## Monday 7th September

```{r graphic for Monday's learning}

knitr::include_graphics("Monday_7_September_work_HWE.png")

```

### 1) Simulate Population & Genotype Data

In this specific code simulation below, we're setting up an idealised, synthetic baseline where no evolutionary forces (drift, select, genotyping error) exist at all.We define true_p = 0.3, so we know the exact ground truth of the population's starting allele frequency.

Using the `rbinom()` function, we generate a population that satisfies HWE assumptions. In real-world data I'll be using in my PhD, you won't know underlying P/MAF. You run HWE to see if observed genotypes differ from expected p-squared, 2pq, q-squared proportions.

Significant deviation would signal: genotyping/calling error in quality-control; populations stratification; inbreeding; strong selection. The object of true_p is included in the `rbinom()` code as it simulates drawing 2 alleles (diploid humans) for each individual, where true_p is the independent probability of alternative allele B on any single draw.

```{r simulating genotypes}

set.seed(123)

n_samples <- 1000

true_p <- 0.3 # The true Minor allele frequency (MAF) of alternative allele 'A'

# Simulate genotypes (0 = 'AA', 1 = 'AB', 2 = 'BB') using Binomial Distribution

#simulating genotypes using binomial distribution
#binomial distribution because each parent contributes 1 allele independently with a set probability#


genotypes <- rbinom(n = n_samples, size = 2, prob = true_p)

 
#generating a factor variable version of the genotypes -
#homozygous dominant, heterozygous, and homozygous recessive

genotype_factor <- factor(genotypes, levels = c(0, 1, 2), labels = c("AA", "AB", "BB"))

```

### 2) Calculate Observed Genotypes & Allele Frequencies

```{r calculating the observed genotypes}

# Count genotypes

obs_counts <- table(genotype_factor)

obs_counts

obs_genotype_freqs <- obs_counts / n_samples

#Calculate allele frequencies#

# The formula is p + q = 1 WRT major and minor allele frequencies# 

#major allele frequency#
p_obs <- (2 * obs_counts["BB"] + obs_counts["AB"]) / (2 * n_samples)

#minor allele frequency#
q_obs <- 1 - p_obs


```

### 3) Calculate Expected HWE Genotype Frequencies

```{r HWE to compute expected frequencies}

exp_genotype_props <- c(
  "AA" = q_obs^2,
  "AB" = 2 * p_obs * q_obs,
  "BB" = p_obs^2
)

# Using the HWE of p^2 + 2pq + q^2 to obtain the expected frequencies#

#This object gives us the expected proportions of homozygous dominant AA, heterozygous AB, and homozygous recessive BB#

#using this step to prevent R concatenating the name of q_obs with AA#
names(exp_genotype_props) <- c("AA", "AB", "BB")
exp_genotype_props

# Multiplying the proportions by the no.samples gives us the actual counts#
exp_counts <- exp_genotype_props * n_samples

exp_counts

```

### 4) Comparing the Observed vs Expected (Using Chi-squared)

```{r Compute Chi-squared test for HWE deviation}

#Using the HardyWeinberg package as it automatically accounts for the parameter estimate, df = 1. 

# The HWChisq() function expects a plain, numeric vector#
#It will fail when calculating the inbreeding coefficient, f, references as fhat#

# Convert obs_counts to a standard numeric vector
counts_vec <- as.numeric(obs_counts)
names(counts_vec) <- c("AA", "AB", "BB")

#Chi-square test with continuity correction for Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (autosomal)#
HWChisq(counts_vec, verbose = TRUE)

```

The p-value is 0.73, you fail to reject the null hypothesis, so the observed genotypes counts match the expected Hardy-Weinberg proportions almost perfectly! We can conclude the genotypes are in random-mating equilibrium within a single generation.

## Thursday 10th September

```{r graphic for Monday's learning}

knitr::include_graphics("Thursday_10th_September_Linear_Reg_Genetic_Associaton.png")

```

Simulating 5K individuals with genotypes 0,1,2 where 0 = AA, 1 = Aa, 2 = aa -

```{r simulating genotypes}

set.seed(123)

n_samples <- 5000

true_p <- 0.3 # The true Minor allele frequency (MAF) of alternative allele 'A'

# Simulate genotypes (0 = 'AA', 1 = 'Aa', 2 = 'aa') using Binomial Distribution

#simulating genotypes using binomial distribution
#binomial distribution because each parent contributes 1 allele independently with a set probability#


genotypes <- rbinom(n = n_samples, size = 2, prob = true_p)

 
#generating a factor variable version of the genotypes -
#homozygous dominant, heterozygous, and homozygous recessive

genotype <- factor(genotypes, levels = c(0, 1, 2), labels = c("AA", "Aa", "aa"))

```

```{r creating the phenotypic object}

#phenotype = baseline + beta 1 coefficient of 2 multiplied by G (genotype object) + random variation E

phenotype <- 50 + (2 * genotypes) + 
  rnorm(length(genotypes), mean = 0,
  sd = 5)

rnorm(length(genotype), mean = 0, sd = 5)

#random variation E is found by generating random numbers from a normal distribution, to get random noise for each individual's genotype#

hist(phenotype)

# the three genotype groups have considerable overlap, with means progressively increasing 

plot(genotype, phenotype)

```

We can see that the 3 genotype groups have considerable overlap, the means progressively increasing.

The important thing they're teaching you is that genotype affects phenotype, but phenotype isn't perfectly determined by genotype because of random variation.

So, we hope the regression will show this relationship as well!



Now, the linear regression model -

```{r lm model}

model <- lm(phenotype ~ genotype)

summary(model)

confint(model)


```
Neither this model (or the one below), contain 0 in a confidence interval. Therefore 0 is not a plausible value for the true effect size - the association between phenotype and genotype is statistically significant!

### Increasing the genetic effect

Below, increasing the genetic effect to see what happens - 

```{r creating the phenotypic object}

#phenotype = baseline + beta 1 coefficient of 2 multiplied by G (genotype object) + random variation E

phenotype_2 <- 50 + (4 * genotypes) + rnorm(length(genotypes), mean = 0,
                                         sd = 5)

rnorm(length(genotype), mean = 0,sd = 5)

#random variation E is found by generating random numbers from a normal distribution, to get random noise for each individual's genotype#

hist(phenotype_2)

# the three genotype groups have considerable overlap, with means progressively increasing 

plot(genotype, phenotype_2)

```


```{r lm model}

model_2 <- lm(phenotype_2 ~ genotype)

summary(model_2)

confint(model_2)

```
In the above model, we see a more bunched up histogram and higher R squared.

Looking at those test statistics, the model output is very small as we've created a strong effect with 1000 individuals. 

I.e. increasing beta-1 has led to a stronger phenotype-genotype relationship and
therefore stronger biological effect!

Questions to investigate, answer:

**(1) What does Beta-1 mean biologically?**

It is the additive genetic effect - important in GWAS.

**(2) What happens when you increase the genetic effect?**

The histogram becomes more 'bunched up' and the R-squared is higher. As beta-1 is increased, the biological effect of each additional allele is stronger.
